body_markdown:
In the cloud era, IaaS meant **Infrastructure-as-a-Service** : rent a server by the hour, run your own software. In the AI era, a new IaaS is taking its place: **Inference-as-a-Service** . You do not rent the server. You rent the *thinking* , billed by the token. Every ChatGPT reply, every agent step, and every AI automation is a purchase from this market, and the companies that sell it are among the fastest-growing businesses in AI.


I spent my teens running web hosting servers out of Queens, and the business model looks familiar. This guide names the category, explains how Inference-as-a-Service works under the hood, shows the unit economics on a real GPU node, and covers what changes when you bring your own key. 🔮


> **TL;DR:** Inference-as-a-Service (IaaS) sells AI model output by the token, the way cloud IaaS sold servers by the hour. An 8-GPU B200 node rents for about **$48/hour** and needs roughly **2,000 output tokens per second** of steady demand to break even on DeepSeek V4 Pro at 2026 prices. Caching, batching, kernels, and custom chips set the margin.[Build AI apps with no GPUs to manage →](https://www.taskade.com/create?entry_kind=content&source=blog&entry=%2Fblog%2Finference-as-a-service)


**Quick answer:** Inference-as-a-Service is how almost every AI product buys model output in 2026. You call an inference API, a provider runs the model on its GPUs or custom chips, and you pay per million tokens. The best LLM inference providers differ less on the model than on speed, cache pricing, uptime terms, and model coverage, so test them on your own prompts.

## What Is Inference-as-a-Service (IaaS)?


**Inference-as-a-Service (IaaS) is the business of running trained AI models and selling their output through an API, priced per million tokens.** The buyer sends a prompt and gets tokens back. The seller owns the hard part: GPUs, batching, caching, kernels, scaling, and uptime. In 2026, IaaS is the layer every AI product is built on, and selling it is a business in its own right.


[Inference](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/inference) is everything a model does after training: it turns your prompt into tokens, runs them through the network, and generates output tokens until the answer is done. Training a frontier model happens once. Inference happens billions of times a day. Inference-as-a-Service is what you get when someone turns that work into a metered utility.


The scale shows up in the revenue charts. In July 2026, investor Deedy Das published a list of AI startups above a $500M revenue run rate, excluding the three biggest labs. Near the top of that list sat companies that mostly serve other people's models: Together AI, Fireworks, and Baseten (inference platforms), plus Lambda and Lightning AI (GPU clouds). Most of the figures were estimates, but the shape was clear. Selling tokens from open-weight models had become one of the fastest ways to build revenue in AI.


That is strange at first glance. The weights of DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, and Qwen are free to download. So what exactly does an IaaS provider sell? The short answer: **turning free weights into fast, reliable, cheap tokens** , which turns out to be very hard. The rest of this guide is the long answer.

## Why Is Inference-as-a-Service the New IaaS?


**Inference-as-a-Service is the new IaaS because it does for AI what Infrastructure-as-a-Service did for software: it turns expensive, idle-prone hardware into a metered utility that anyone can rent.** The acronym is the same on purpose. Cloud IaaS sold servers by the hour. AI IaaS sells model output by the token, one layer higher in the stack.


Every era of computing has had a "rent it instead of owning it" layer. Each one moved the unit of sale closer to the outcome the customer wanted:


Era What you rent Unit of sale Who runs the hardware


Web hosting (1990s–2000s) A share of a server Per account, per month The host


Infrastructure-as-a-Service (2006+) Virtual machines, storage, networks Per hour The cloud


Platform-as-a-Service (2008+) A place to deploy your code Per app, per request The cloud


Software-as-a-Service (2000s+) Finished software Per seat, per month The vendor


**Inference-as-a-Service (2023+)** **A trained model's output** **Per million tokens** **The model host**


Inference-as-a-Service is not SaaS, even though both are sold through the browser and the API. The difference is in the cost of the next customer:

What the customer buys Finished software Model output

Cost of one more user Close to zero Real GPU time on every request


Where the margin comes from Reuse of the same code Utilization, caching, kernels, and chips


Typical gross margin High Thin and volatile


What wins Product and distribution Cost per token and reliability


That last row is the whole story of this guide. SaaS margins come from software that costs nothing to copy. IaaS margins come from squeezing more tokens out of every GPU-hour. The two layers need each other: AI apps are the SaaS of this era, and they run on Inference-as-a-Service the way the last generation of SaaS ran on cloud infrastructure.

## How Does LLM Inference Work, Step by Step?


**An inference request moves through five steps: tokenize the prompt, prefill it, store its KV cache, decode the answer one token at a time, and stream the text back.** The first two steps happen once per request. The decode loop repeats for every output token, which is why long answers cost more than long questions.


Each step has a cost owner. The tokenizer is nearly free. Prefill is a big burst of matrix math. The KV cache is memory you rent by the gigabyte-second. Decode is a long, slow loop that rereads the model's weights for every token. Streaming is the part the user sees, measured as time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT).


The[transformer](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/transformer) architecture makes this loop possible, and its attention mechanism makes it expensive. Each new token "looks back" at every token before it, which is exactly what the KV cache stores so the model does not recompute it.

## What Is the Difference Between Prefill and Decode?


**Prefill reads the entire prompt in one parallel pass and is limited by compute, while decode writes one token at a time and is limited by memory bandwidth.** A GPU can prefill 10,000 tokens in roughly the time it takes to decode a few dozen. That asymmetry sets prices: providers typically charge two to six times more for an output token than for an input token.


Think of prefill as reading a book and decode as writing a letter by hand. You can skim a whole chapter in seconds because your eyes take in many words at once. But you can only write one word at a time, and before each word you glance back over everything you have written so far.


Prefill Decode


What it does Reads the whole prompt Writes the answer, one token per step


Parallel? Yes, all prompt tokens at once No, each token depends on the last


Bottleneck Raw compute (FLOPs)[Memory bandwidth](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/infrastructure/memory-bandwidth)


What it fills The KV cache Reads the KV cache plus all weights, every step


User-visible metric Time to first token Tokens per second while streaming


Typical price Input rate Output rate, 2x to 6x the input rate


```text
ONE REQUEST ON ONE GPU, OVER TIME
┌──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PREFILL  │ DECODE  DECODE  DECODE  DECODE  DECODE  DECODE  │
│ 10,000   │  tok 1   tok 2   tok 3   tok 4   tok 5   ...    │
│ tokens,  │                                                 │
│ one pass │ each step reloads the weights + the KV cache    │
│          │ from HBM, then does very little math with them  │
└──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
compute-bound           memory-bandwidth-bound
(GPU cores busy)        (GPU cores mostly waiting)


```


This is the single most important idea in inference economics. During decode, the expensive math units of a GPU spend most of their time waiting for data to arrive from[high-bandwidth memory](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/infrastructure/hbm) . Every optimization in the rest of this guide is a way to make that waiting cheaper: share it across more users (batching), skip it (caching), shorten it (kernels and quantization), or remove it (chips that keep weights in on-chip SRAM).

**Five kinds of company sell Inference-as-a-Service in 2026: model labs, hyperscalers, neoclouds, full-stack inference platforms, and custom-silicon companies.** Only the last two treat serving open models as their core business. Model labs such as DeepSeek, OpenAI, and Anthropic serve their own models first, and they set the price every other IaaS provider is measured against.

### Inference platforms: Together AI, Fireworks AI, Baseten, DeepInfra


**An AI inference platform sells serving software as the product: it takes open weights on launch day and races to make them fast and cheap.** All four offer a per-token API for popular open models and a dedicated option for steady traffic. They differ in emphasis. Together AI and Fireworks AI lead with catalog breadth and tuning paths, Baseten leads with custom models and deployment choices (its own cloud, your VPC, or both), and DeepInfra leads with low prices and dedicated clusters it operates itself.


Baseten is also a useful case of day-zero work. Its engineers described standing up a Kimi K3 API on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems, 8 GPUs per replica, on the day the open weights shipped. That is the job an inference platform sells: the weights are free, and the serving work is not.


### Custom silicon: Groq and Cerebras


**Groq and Cerebras sell speed per user, not breadth.** Both keep model weights in on-chip SRAM instead of HBM, which removes the memory wait that slows decode on a GPU. The section oncustom chips below compares them with an NVIDIA B200. On October 20, 2026, Cerebras's public model list showed two models, gpt-oss-120b and Qwen 3.8 27B. So check the catalog before you plan around either chip.


### Neocloud with a token API: Nebius


**Nebius sits between a GPU cloud and an inference platform.** It rents raw GPU capacity, and its Token Factory sells an OpenAI-compatible model API with dedicated endpoints and batch jobs. On Kimi K3 it measured among the fastest hosts in October 2026, as thehost-speed chart below shows.


### Hyperscalers: Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry


**Hyperscalers sell inference as one line on a cloud bill you already pay.** Their edge is the contract, not the token price: existing security reviews, data residency options, private networking, and committed-spend discounts. Amazon Bedrock states that it never stores or uses your data to train models. Microsoft Foundry offers regional, data-zone, and global processing. Vertex AI Model Garden serves open models as a managed service next to Google's own models. For a team inside one cloud, that convenience often outweighs a faster host elsewhere.

## Serverless Inference vs Dedicated Endpoints vs Self-Hosting


**Serverless inference bills per token on a shared endpoint, a dedicated endpoint bills per GPU-hour or reserved capacity on hardware that serves only you, and self-hosting means you run an open-source model on GPUs you rent or own.** Most teams start serverless, move steady traffic to dedicated capacity, and self-host only when volume, data rules, or a custom model demand it.


The choice is a trade between flexibility and utilization. A serverless endpoint is shared by many customers, so the provider keeps the batch full and you pay only for tokens you use. A dedicated endpoint is yours alone, so you pay for idle time too, but you get steadier latency and no noisy neighbors. Self-hosting puts the whole serving stack from this guide on your team.

That state diagram is the hidden cost of a dedicated endpoint that scales to zero. The first request after a quiet period waits for the weights to load into GPU memory, which for a model the size of Kimi K3 means moving about 1.56 TB. Serverless endpoints avoid the cold start because someone else's traffic keeps the model warm, and that shared warmth is part of what you pay for in the per-token price.


### What is an inference API?


**An inference API is the HTTP endpoint you send a prompt to and stream tokens back from.** Most providers in 2026 accept the OpenAI chat completions format, so moving between hosts usually means changing three values: the base URL, the API key, and the model name. Groq, for example, documents` https://api.groq.com/openai/v1` as its OpenAI-compatible base URL.


Bash


```text
# An OpenAI-compatible inference API call. Swap the base URL, key, and model name per host.
curl https://api.your-provider.example/v1/chat/completions \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $PROVIDER_API_KEY" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"model": "provider-specific/model-name",
"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this contract in five bullets."}],
"max_tokens": 400,
"stream": true
}'


```


"Compatible" rarely means identical. Hosts differ on which parameters they accept, how they report cached tokens, how they name the same model, and how they return tool calls. Run your real prompts, including tool calls and structured output, on each candidate before you switch traffic.


### Open source model hosting: what you take on when you self-host


**Self-hosting an open-weight model means you own the serving engine, the GPU fleet, and the uptime.** Open engines such as[vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) and SGLang do most of the hard work covered in this guide, including continuous batching, PagedAttention, and prefix caching. Kubernetes-based schedulers such as llm-d add routing and disaggregation across nodes. KodeKloud's explainer walks through that stack, from GPUs to vLLM to llm-d:


The software is free. The hard part is keeping it full. Before you self-host, size the job with the same numbers a provider uses:

## What Are the Unit Economics of Inference-as-a-Service?


**The unit of Inference-as-a-Service is the GPU-hour, and the product is tokens: an 8-GPU B200 node rents for about $48 an hour and needs roughly 2,000 output tokens per second of steady demand to break even on DeepSeek V4 Pro at 2026 prices.** A basic open-source vLLM setup on the same node measures about 912 tokens per second. The gap between those two numbers is the whole IaaS business.

So at the 2:1 workload shape, the basic setup earns less than half its rent. The Lambda run used a heavier mix, 4 input tokens for every output token. Priced at that mix, 4 × $1.74 + $3.48 = $10.44 per 1M output tokens of work, the same run earns about $34 an hour, or about 70% of the rent. At either mix the node loses money, and that is before CPUs, storage, networking, engineers, and idle hours. Two more facts make it harder:


1. **Per-user speed falls as you pack more users in.** Lambda's run gave each user about 28.5 tokens per second. To reach 2,000 total, the node must serve roughly 70 streams at once at that speed, and bigger batches tend to make each stream slower.
2. **Demand is not constant.** Traffic peaks in business hours and drops at night. A node that is half idle has to earn its rent in half the time.

That 545% figure is the ceiling the whole industry chases. It shows what a lab can do on its own model with its own kernels. The rest of this guide explains the levers that close the gap between 912 and 14,800.

## Why Can't Third-Party IaaS Providers Beat the Lab's Own Price?


**Labs usually win on price for their own models because they tune kernels for the exact model shapes before launch, they see their real production traffic, and they can price below cost to win share.** A third party starts on launch day, must reverse-engineer the bottlenecks, and has to make a profit on every token.


DeepSeek's pricing history in 2026 shows how the lab sets the frame for everyone:

The spread across hosts can be even wider for a model with no first-party API. MIRI's technology governance team found Llama 3.1 405B priced from $0.90 to $9.50 per million tokens across providers, with a median near $3.50. Same weights, a 10x price range.


Look at what that means for an inference platform. For months, the lab sold V4 Pro at a quarter of the price that the third parties needed to break even. No amount of software tuning fixes a 4x price gap on the same weights. So third parties pick their battles: models whose labs lack compute, customers who need a region or a contract the lab cannot offer, and workloads where steady latency matters more than the lowest price.


Compute shortages create those openings. On July 19, 2026, Moonshot temporarily paused new Kimi subscriptions ([South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/tech/article/3361172/kimi-k3-developer-suspends-new-subscriptions-amid-compute-constraints) ). In its announcement, the lab said that demand for Kimi K3 was approaching the limits of its existing GPU clusters, and that it would give compute to current paid subscribers first. When a lab cannot serve its own users, every inference platform hosting the same weights becomes the overflow. Read the[Moonshot and Kimi history](https://www.taskade.com/blog/moonshot-kimi-history) and the[DeepSeek history](https://www.taskade.com/blog/deepseek-ai-history) for the labs' side of this story.

## Case study: one 8x B300 node serving Kimi K3


**Kimi K3 is a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model with about 104 billion parameters active per token, and its 1.56 TB checkpoint fits on one 8x NVIDIA B300 node but not on an 8x B200 node.** That single fact sets the hardware bill before any software tuning starts. It also shows why a host buys memory for the total parameter count, not the active one.


Moonshot opened the Kimi K3 API on July 16, 2026, and published the open weights and the tech report on July 27, 2026, under its own Kimi K3 License. Here is the model a host has to fit:

### Why total parameters, not active ones, set the memory bill


Only about 3.7% of Kimi K3's weights work on any one token, so it is tempting to think a host needs a fraction of the memory. It does not. At production batch sizes, dozens of requests are in flight, and between them every expert is active at some instant. Moving experts in and out of GPU memory on demand would break the latency targets a host promises, so all 896 experts stay resident.

### TP8 or TP plus expert parallelism


Once the weights fit, the host chooses how to split them across the 8 GPUs. **Tensor parallelism (TP8)** shards every layer across all 8 GPUs. It gives the best latency for a single user, but every layer ends in collective traffic between the GPUs. **TP plus expert parallelism (EP)** keeps attention sharded the same way but places whole experts on specific GPUs. It cuts the collective traffic that TP8 pays on every layer and gives better total throughput.


Expert parallelism has one weak spot: real traffic does not spread evenly. Some experts get far more tokens than others, and the GPU that holds them becomes the bottleneck. **Expert load balancing** fixes that at run time. The engine watches which experts are hot and adds or removes replicas of them, so the load stays even across the node.

## Why Does Prompt Caching Make AI So Much Cheaper?


**Prompt caching reuses the KV cache of a prompt prefix the server has already read, so a repeated system prompt, tool list, or conversation history skips most of prefill.** Providers pass the saving on: Anthropic bills cache reads at 0.1x of normal input, and DeepSeek bills a cache hit at about 3% of a miss. For agents, caching is the biggest single line on the bill.


When a server reads a prompt for the first time, that is a **cache miss** : it runs every token through every layer and stores the result. When a later request starts with the same tokens, that is a **cache hit** : the server loads the stored state and only prefills the new part. Coding agents and[AI agents](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-are-ai-agents) resend the same instructions, tools, and history on every step, so most of their input can be cache hits.

Caching is also why DeepSeek's headline throughput was so high. In its March 2025 report, **342 billion of 608 billion input tokens in one day (56.3%) were cache hits** from an on-disk KV cache, and the 73.7k tokens-per-second figure counted them. Real production traffic reuses a lot.


The rule for builders is simple: **keep the long, shared part of the prompt identical, and put anything that changes at the end.** A timestamp at the top of a system prompt can silently turn every request into a cache miss. The[prompt caching](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/prompt-caching) and[inference cost](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/inference-cost) wiki pages go deeper, and[How to Reduce LLM Costs](https://www.taskade.com/blog/reduce-llm-costs) covers the practical tactics.


### Why prefix caching gets coarser on hybrid models


**On a hybrid model such as Kimi K3, a cached prefix is reused only from the nearest saved checkpoint of the linear-attention state, not to the exact token.** The model keeps two kinds of attention memory, and only one of them can be cut at any token.


Kimi K3's 24 Gated MLA layers keep a per-token cache: 576 values per layer, about 13.5 KiB per token in FP8 across those layers. That cache grows with every token, and a matching prefix can be reused to the exact token, as on any transformer. The 69 KDA layers keep no per-token cache at all. Each sequence holds one fixed-size recurrent state instead, about 217 MB in BF16 across the model, or about 27 MB per GPU at TP8.


Gated MLA layers (24) KDA layers (69)


What they store Keys and values for every token One running state per sequence


Size About 13.5 KiB per token in FP8, grows with context About 217 MB in BF16, flat at any length


Prefix reuse To the exact token From the nearest saved state checkpoint


Memory pool Its own allocator A second allocator


A recurrent state summarizes every token read so far, so it cannot be rewound to an earlier token. To reuse a prefix, the server needs a copy of the state saved at some point inside it. Servers save those copies at intervals, resume from the nearest one, and prefill the rest again. The engine runs two allocators side by side, one for each kind of memory. The rule for builders does not change, but it matters more on hybrid models: a long, identical prefix leaves more room for a saved checkpoint inside it.

## What Is Continuous Batching and Why Is It the Business Model?


**Continuous batching lets one GPU serve many users at once by adding new requests and removing finished ones at every decode step.** Because decode is limited by memory, not math, one load of the model's weights can serve dozens of users almost as cheaply as one. More demand means bigger batches, and bigger batches mean a lower cost per token.


Early serving systems used static batches: collect a group of requests, run them together, and wait until the longest answer finished. Short answers sat idle while long ones kept going. In 2022 the Orca paper (OSDI) introduced iteration-level scheduling and reported 36.9x the throughput of NVIDIA FasterTransformer on a GPT-3-scale model at the same latency. The idea became standard in vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM.


Batch size (simultaneous users) Weight loads per decode step Cost per token User experience


1 1 load serves 1 user Highest Fastest per user, wasteful


32 1 load serves 32 users Much lower Still fast (about 28 tokens/s each in Lambda's B200 test)


70+ 1 load serves 70+ users Near break-even on the node above Slower per user, longer queues


Very large Limited by KV cache memory Lowest, until memory runs out Long time to first token


This is why scale compounds in inference. A provider with millions of requests can keep every batch full at any hour. A provider with a few customers pays for idle GPUs. The trade-off never goes away: a bigger batch raises total throughput but makes each user wait longer and uses more KV cache memory. Providers tune that dial all day.


[PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180) , introduced with vLLM in 2023, made big batches practical. It stores the KV cache in small fixed-size pages, the way an operating system manages memory, so the server wastes far less GPU memory and fits more users per node. The paper reported 2x to 4x the throughput of earlier systems at the same latency.

## What Is Prefill-Decode Disaggregation?


**Prefill-decode disaggregation runs the two stages on separate pools of GPUs: one pool reads prompts, the other writes answers, and the KV cache moves between them over a fast network.** Each pool scales on its own, and a giant prompt no longer stalls everyone else's decode.


Because prefill wants raw compute and decode wants memory bandwidth and big batches, running both on the same GPU is a compromise. Research systems such as Splitwise (2023) and DistServe (2024) split them. DistServe reported serving up to 7.4x more requests within the same latency targets. Moonshot's Mooncake (2024) built a KV-cache-centric architecture around the same idea, and Moonshot reported that it handled 75% more requests in production. In April 2026 Moonshot and Tsinghua proposed **Prefill-as-a-Service** : send long-context prefill to a separate data center, then ship the finished KV cache back to the decode cluster.


For a buyer, disaggregation shows up as steadier time to first token on long prompts. For a provider, it is one more way to keep expensive hardware doing the work it is best at.


The traffic mix decides how big each pool gets. Agentic and long-context traffic sends long prompts and gets short answers back: an agent can resend a long history of instructions, tool results, and files just to write one short tool call. So for that traffic, hosts tend to add prefill capacity rather than decode capacity. Chat traffic with long answers pulls the other way.


### Speculative decoding speeds up the decode pool


**Speculative decoding raises per-user tokens per second by letting a small speculator draft several tokens that the big model then checks in one pass.** Decode is limited by memory bandwidth, so checking several drafted tokens costs about as much as writing one. Every accepted draft token is a nearly free extra token. Three recent designs:


Speculator How it drafts Paper


EAGLE-3 Drafts from the target model's own hidden states arXiv 2503.01840 (2025)


DFlash A block-diffusion speculator that drafts a block of tokens at once arXiv 2602.06036 (2026)


DSpark Semi-autoregressive drafting, with a verify length set per request by confidence arXiv 2607.05147 (2026)


Speculators train on the target model's hidden states, so the model must run in production first. A new open model can launch on day one without a tuned speculator and get faster on the same host once one is trained.

## What Are Custom Kernels and Why Do Labs Serve Their Own Models Faster?


**A GPU kernel is a small program that tells thousands of GPU threads what to compute and how to move data. A custom kernel is written for one model's exact shapes, precision, and hardware.** Most of the speedup comes from moving less data, not from doing less math, and labs can write their kernels before the model is public.


When you write one line of PyTorch, the framework launches one or more general-purpose kernels. They work on any model, so they are rarely perfect for any one model. A serving team replaces the hot paths with specialized kernels using a few techniques:


Technique What it does Why it is faster


Kernel fusion Combines steps such as normalize, quantize, and multiply into one kernel Skips writing and rereading intermediate results in HBM


Tiling Splits big matrices into blocks that fit the fastest on-chip memory Each block is reused many times before it leaves the chip


[FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) (2022) Computes attention in tiles and never stores the full attention matrix in HBM Same result, far less memory traffic; 3x faster GPT-2 training in the original paper


Quantization (FP8, FP4) Stores weights in fewer bits Less data to move per token; DeepSeek V4 Pro ships FP4 experts


[Mixture-of-experts](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/mixture-of-experts) routing kernels Sends each token only to the experts it needs Only 49B of V4 Pro's 1.6T parameters work on each token


Speculative decoding (2022) A small model drafts several tokens and the big model checks them at once Turns idle decode compute into extra tokens, 2x to 3x faster with identical output in the original paper


Custom kernels are also why the same open weights run at very different speeds on different hosts. The lab knows how many experts fire per token, where its quantization loses accuracy, and where GPU-to-GPU communication stalls. A third party learns those things after launch. Until it does, the same model needs more GPUs, produces fewer tokens per second, and costs more to serve. The catch: custom kernels are hard to write, hard to debug, and fast only for the shapes they were built for. A kernel tuned for an H100 can be slow on a B200.

### Rate limits are part of the SLA


**A rate limit is a quiet SLA term: it caps how many requests or tokens per minute your key can send, and a request over the cap fails with an HTTP 429 error.** Serverless tiers set limits per key and often per model, and limits tighten when a host runs short of capacity at peak hours. Reserved and dedicated tiers raise them. Build retries with backoff, and keep a second host or a second key ready for the hours when the first one says no.


### How to test latency and throughput yourself


**The only benchmark that predicts your bill and your users' wait is one run on your own prompts.** Public leaderboards are a starting point, because they use a fixed prompt length and a fixed time window. A short test on two or three hosts takes an afternoon:


1. **Collect 50 to 100 real prompts** from your app, with their real system prompts, tool lists, and context lengths.
2. **Send each prompt to every candidate host** with the same settings, and stream the answers.
3. **Record time to first token, output tokens per second, and total time** for every request, plus every error.
4. **Report the median and the 99th percentile** , not the average.
5. **Repeat at your peak hour** , because a host that is fast at night can queue at noon.
6. **Read the bill** , including the cached-input line, because cache hits change the real price per task.

## Where Is Inference-as-a-Service Going Next?


**The Inference-as-a-Service market is splitting into labs that train models and companies that serve them, and that split is likely to widen.** Many labs lack the compute to train frontier models and serve global demand at the same time, and export limits make high-end GPUs even harder to get for some of them. Every GPU spent serving is one GPU not training the next model.


Five trends to watch:


1. **Serving specialists grow with open weights.** As open models close the gap with closed ones, demand to have them served grows with them.
2. **Prices fall, but not in a straight line.** Labs run promotions, raise prices when compute is tight, and add off-peak discounts. DeepSeek did all three in 2026.
3. **Caching becomes the main price line.** For agents, cached input is already most of the tokens. Expect longer cache lifetimes and cheaper cache reads.
4. **Prefill moves.** Disaggregation inside a data center is standard. Moving prefill across data centers, as Prefill-as-a-Service proposes, is next.
5. **Apps stop reselling tokens.** BYOK lets customers bring the inference contract they already have, and apps compete on what they build on top.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What is LLM inference?


LLM inference is the work a trained large language model does when you use it. The model reads your prompt, runs it through its neural network, and generates an answer one token at a time. Training builds the model once. Inference runs every time anyone sends a prompt, so in 2026 it is where most of the money in AI is spent and earned.


What is the difference between prefill and decode?


Prefill is the first stage of inference: the model reads the whole prompt at once, in parallel, which is limited by raw compute. Decode is the second stage: the model writes the answer one token at a time, and each token depends on the one before it, which is limited by memory bandwidth. That difference is why output tokens cost several times more than input tokens.


What is a KV cache and why does prompt caching make AI cheaper?


The KV cache stores the attention keys and values the model computed for every token it has already read. When a new request starts with the same prefix, such as the same system prompt and tool list, the server can reuse that cache instead of reading the prefix again. Providers pass the saving on: Anthropic bills cache reads at 0.1x of the normal input price, and DeepSeek bills cache hits at about 3 percent of a cache miss.


What is Inference-as-a-Service (IaaS)?


Inference-as-a-Service (IaaS) is the business of running trained AI models on GPUs or custom chips and selling the output through an API, priced per million tokens. You send a prompt and get tokens back, and the provider handles hardware, batching, caching, and scaling. Sellers include model labs serving their own models, hyperscalers, GPU clouds, inference platforms such as Fireworks, Together AI, and Baseten, and custom-silicon companies such as Groq and Cerebras.


How is Inference-as-a-Service different from Infrastructure-as-a-Service?


Infrastructure-as-a-Service, the original IaaS from the cloud era, rents raw servers, storage, and networks by the hour, and you run your own software on them. Inference-as-a-Service rents the result of running an AI model, billed per token, and the provider runs the model for you. The acronym is the same because the job is the same one layer up: turn expensive hardware into a metered utility.


Is Inference-as-a-Service a SaaS business?


Not quite. SaaS sells finished software by the seat, with high gross margins because each extra user costs little. Inference-as-a-Service sells metered compute by the token, and every token burns GPU time, so margins depend on utilization, caching, and hardware cost. AI apps sit on top of IaaS the way SaaS products sit on top of cloud infrastructure.


What are the best LLM inference providers in 2026?


The best provider depends on the workload. Together AI, Fireworks AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra serve a broad catalog of open models. Groq and Cerebras lead on per-user speed for the models they support. Nebius Token Factory pairs a model API with dedicated GPUs, and Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry suit teams that need cloud contracts and compliance. Speed varies by host even for the same weights, so test with your own prompts.


What is serverless inference?


Serverless inference means you call a shared, always-on model endpoint and pay per token, with no GPUs to reserve, load, or scale. The provider serves many customers from the same fleet, so it is the cheapest way to start and the easiest way to absorb spiky traffic. Steady, high-volume, or latency-critical work often moves to dedicated endpoints or provisioned throughput, billed per GPU-hour or per reserved capacity.


What is an inference API?


An inference API is the HTTP endpoint you send prompts to and stream tokens back from. Most providers in 2026 accept the OpenAI chat completions format, so switching hosts usually means changing three things: the base URL, the API key, and the model name. Groq documents its API as mostly compatible with OpenAI client libraries, and Cerebras says its API needs two code changes.


Is it cheaper to self-host an open-source model or use an inference API?


For most teams an inference API is cheaper, because you pay only for tokens you use and the provider keeps the GPUs full. Self-hosting pays off with high, steady volume, strict data residency, or a custom model. As a reference point, an 8-GPU B200 node rents for about 48 dollars an hour and needs roughly 2,000 output tokens per second of steady demand to break even on DeepSeek V4 Pro at 2026 prices.


Which inference provider is fastest for Kimi K3?


On October 20, 2026, Artificial Analysis measured LithosAI Ultra Chat at about 422 output tokens per second on Kimi K3, followed by Parasail at about 198 and Nebius at about 192. Amazon Bedrock measured about 142, Fireworks about 112, Baseten about 96, Together AI about 57, and Moonshot's own API about 42. The numbers are 72-hour medians and change weekly, so check the live page before you choose.


What SLA should I ask an inference provider for?


Ask for a written uptime percentage, how it is measured, and the credit you get when it is missed, plus time to first token and output speed at your prompt length at the median and the 99th percentile. A 99.9 percent monthly SLA allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month, and 99.99 percent allows about 4 minutes. Reserved or dedicated tiers usually carry the strongest terms.


How do inference providers make money if anyone can download open-weight models?


They make money on the gap between what a GPU-hour costs and how many tokens they can sell from it. A basic 8-GPU B200 node costs roughly 48 dollars an hour to rent, and at 2026 list prices it needs about 2,000 output tokens per second of steady demand just to break even on DeepSeek V4 Pro. Caching, batching, custom kernels, and custom chips are how providers get above that line.


Why do output tokens cost more than input tokens?


Input tokens are processed in parallel during prefill, so a GPU reads thousands of them in one pass. Output tokens are generated one at a time during decode, and every step must reload model weights and the KV cache from memory. Decode uses far more GPU time per token, so providers typically price output at two to six times the input rate.


What is continuous batching?


Continuous batching lets an inference server add new requests and remove finished ones at every decode step instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish. It keeps the GPU full while users send prompts of different lengths. It was introduced as iteration-level scheduling in the Orca paper in 2022 and is standard in vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM.


Are Groq and Cerebras faster than GPUs for inference?


For per-user speed on supported models, yes. On gpt-oss-120b, Artificial Analysis measured Cerebras at roughly 1,600 to 1,800 output tokens per second per user in 2026 and Groq at about 474, several times faster than typical GPU hosts. The trade-off is model coverage: a new, complex architecture can take a long time to reach custom silicon.
